title: Given a Scenario, Configure and Apply Basic Microsoft Windows OS Security Settings

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Windows provides built-in controls for malware, network traffic, accounts, sign-in, authorization, privilege elevation, encryption, and centralized domain management.
Use this mental model: protect → authenticate → authorize → encrypt → manage.
bullets: NTFS and share permissions, elevation, and UAC

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a Windows security scenario appears, decide whether the required control scans malware, filters traffic, changes an account or sign-in method, applies permissions, elevates a process, encrypts data, or manages the domain.
sections.callout: Malware → Defender; traffic → Firewall; elevation prompt → UAC; drive → BitLocker; removable drive → BitLocker-To-Go; file or folder → EFS.

sections.title: Defender Antivirus
paragraphs: Microsoft Defender Antivirus supplies built-in antimalware protection.

entries.title: Activate/Deactivate
paragraphs: Turn the antimalware engine on or off through Windows Security. Protection normally remains active unless an approved troubleshooting or management need requires otherwise.

entries.title: Update Definitions
paragraphs: Current security intelligence and signatures help Defender recognize newly identified threats.
entries.recognitionCue: Protection is enabled but signatures are stale → update definitions.

sections.title: Firewall
paragraphs: Windows Firewall filters inbound and outbound network traffic.

entries.title: Activate/Deactivate
paragraphs: Enable or disable the firewall for the applicable network profile; keep it enabled during normal operation.

entries.title: Port Security
paragraphs: Permit or deny traffic by port and protocol.
entries.recognitionCue: A service requires an inbound TCP port → configure a port rule.

entries.title: Application Security
paragraphs: Allow or block a specific application rather than opening unrelated traffic.
entries.recognitionCue: An app needs network access → application rule or exception.

entries.title: Local vs. Microsoft Account
paragraphs: A local account exists on one PC. A Microsoft account is cloud connected and integrates Windows with Microsoft services.

entries.title: Standard Account
paragraphs: Supports everyday work without unrestricted administrative rights and aligns with least privilege.

entries.title: Administrator
paragraphs: Can make elevated, system-wide changes; these rights should be used only when required.

entries.title: Guest User
paragraphs: Provides limited temporary access when supported and enabled.

entries.title: Power User
paragraphs: A legacy intermediate-privilege group or concept. Modern Windows primarily uses standard users, administrators, and UAC.

entries.title: Username and Password
paragraphs: Traditional sign-in using a named identity and a memorized secret.

entries.title: Personal Identification Number (PIN)
paragraphs: A short, device-bound sign-in secret used by Windows Hello.

entries.title: Fingerprint
paragraphs: Biometric sign-in using a supported fingerprint reader.

entries.title: Facial Recognition
paragraphs: Biometric sign-in using a supported camera.

entries.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
paragraphs: One authentication provides access to multiple authorized resources.

entries.title: Passwordless/Windows Hello
paragraphs: Modern Windows sign-in using a PIN, fingerprint, or facial recognition instead of transmitting a reusable password.
entries.recognitionCue: PIN or biometric Windows login → Windows Hello.

entries.title: NTFS Permissions
paragraphs: Authorize access to files and folders on an NTFS volume for both local and network access.

entries.title: Share Permissions
paragraphs: Apply when a resource is reached through a network share.

entries.title: Effective Network Access
paragraphs: When NTFS and share permissions both apply, their combined effect constrains access; the more restrictive effective permission wins.

sections.title: File and Folder Attributes and Inheritance

entries.title: File and Folder Attributes
paragraphs: Read-only, hidden, and archive are properties of files and folders; they are not NTFS authorization permissions.

entries.title: Inheritance
paragraphs: Allows permissions from a parent folder to flow to child folders and files.
entries.recognitionCue: A new file receives its folder's permissions → inheritance.

sections.title: Run as Administrator and User Account Control

entries.title: Run as Administrator vs. Standard User
paragraphs: A standard user runs with normal rights. Run as administrator requests elevated execution for a process that needs system-level access.

entries.title: User Account Control (UAC)
paragraphs: Prompts for consent or credentials when a task requests elevated privileges.
entries.recognitionCue: Installer triggers an elevation confirmation → UAC.

sections.callout: Administrator describes an account's privilege level; UAC is the elevation control and prompt.

entries.title: BitLocker
paragraphs: Encrypts a Windows volume to protect data if a device or internal drive is lost or stolen.

entries.title: BitLocker-To-Go
paragraphs: Encrypts removable storage such as USB drives.

entries.title: Encrypting File System (EFS)
paragraphs: Encrypts selected files and folders on NTFS.

sections.title: Active Directory
paragraphs: Active Directory centrally manages users, computers, groups, resources, authentication, and policy in a Windows domain.

entries.title: Joining a Domain
paragraphs: Adds a Windows computer to central domain identity and policy management.

entries.title: Assigning Log-In Script
paragraphs: Runs a script when a user signs in to map drives, configure resources, or run required commands.

entries.title: Moving Objects Within Organizational Units
paragraphs: Organizational units arrange users, computers, and groups; moving an object can change administrative or Group Policy scope.

entries.title: Assigning Home Folders
paragraphs: Provides a user-specific network storage location.

entries.title: Applying Group Policy
paragraphs: Centrally configures user and computer security settings, restrictions, desktop behavior, and scripts.

entries.title: Selecting Security Groups
paragraphs: Assigns authorization to group membership instead of managing permissions one user at a time.

entries.title: Configuring Folder Redirection
paragraphs: Points standard user folders to another location, often central network storage.

table.caption: Choose the matching Active Directory feature
rows: Make a PC part of centralized management
Run an action when a user signs in
Organize objects and scope administration or policy
Give a user dedicated network storage
Move known user folders to central storage

sections.title: Security Configuration Workflow
bullets: Identify whether the issue is malware, traffic, identity, authorization, elevation, encryption, or domain management.
Apply the narrowest control that satisfies the requirement.
Preserve least privilege and avoid unnecessary firewall openings or administrator use.
Verify the setting and test the intended user, application, or resource access.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Modern PIN or biometric login → Windows Hello
Central Windows identity and policy → Active Directory

sections.title: Objective 2.2 Exam Trap
bullets: Defender handles malware; Firewall handles network traffic.
A local account belongs to one PC; a Microsoft account is cloud connected.
Run as administrator requests elevation; UAC controls and prompts for it.
NTFS permissions apply at the filesystem; share permissions apply through the network share.
BitLocker protects a volume, BitLocker-To-Go protects removable storage, and EFS protects selected files or folders.
An OU organizes and scopes policy; a security group assigns access.
A home folder is user-specific storage; folder redirection moves known folder paths.
